issues.body:
Judge has assessed an item in Issue #883 as 3 risk. The relevant finding follows:

 As such, if deposit() or withdraw() reverts for any derivative, stake() and unstake() will fail.

This could cause stake() and unstake() to permanently revert for an prolonged period of time, as it is possible for deposit() and withdraw() to revert due to unchecked external conditions:

Reth
The rocket pool DAO can disable deposits.
Withdrawals will fail if rocket pool does not have sufficient ETH.
WstETH
stETH has a daily staking limit, which could cause deposits to fail.
If any of the external conditions above occurs, their respecitve function will be DOSed.

Although an owner can prevent this by setting the affected derivative's weight to 0, this is not a sufficient mitigation as:

This affects the ETH distribution for each derivative, potentially making it unbalanced.
If the DOS is over a short period of time but occurs repeatedly, such as stETH's staking limit, the owner will have to keep adjusting the affected derivative's weight.

issues.title: All the STeth balance of WstEth contract can be drained by a malicious user.
Reth griefing
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L171-L175


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The maximum slippage when buying rETH from the Uniswap V3 pool is calculated in Reth derivative contract by taking the current price in the Uniswap V3 pool at runtime, without taking into account the price at which the user sent the transaction to the mempool:
```
uint rethPerEth = (10 ** 36) / poolPrice();
uint256 minOut = ((((rethPerEth * msg.value) / 10 ** 18) *
    ((10 ** 18 - maxSlippage))) / 10 ** 18);
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L171-L175

Thus, a malicious actor can create a sandwich of three transactions in which they first raise the price of rETH, then execute the user's `stake()` with a purchase of rETH at an unfavorable price, and then return the pool price to normal.

The victim will receive fewer shares than expected. Firstly, because the `underlyingValue` in the `stake()` function will increase due to the fact that `Reth.poolPrice()` will return an inflated value. Secondly, because `Reth.deposit()` will return a smaller amount of rETH when purchasing from the UniswapV3 pool.


## Tools Used

x


## Recommended Mitigation Steps


The slippage should be calculated and controlled by the user before submitting a `stake()` transaction to mempool. For example, `minOut` can be passed as an argument to the `stake()` function.

issues.title: Users might lose their stETH rebased reward due to the weights change
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L108-L129


# Vulnerability details

## Vulnerability Details
* Let's consider the following scenario:
  * Bob deposits 10eth with the weights:
    * stETH: `weights[0] = 90e18,`
    * rETH: `weights[1] = 5e18.`
    * sfrxETH: `weights[2] = 5e18`

  * Now, since the Lido has 80% of liquid staking market, Asymmetry Finance decides to adjust the weights and set 0% for Lido. Over the time the balance of the wstETH derivative becomes close to 0.
  * After that, Bob decides to unstake his shares, but he doesn't receive any rewards occuered on his initial 90% of stETH. Instead, he receives some eth from RocketPool and Frax, which is not comparable with the amount that he could receive back, if the weights were unchanged over the time.

* Initially Bob receives the following amount of shares:
    * X amount of shares for 90% of eth (deposited into the Lido)
    * Y amount of shares for 5% of eth (deposited into the RocketPool)
    * Z amount of shares for 5% of eth (deposited into the Frax)

</br>

* After changing the weights and the balances are also adjusted, Bob doesn't receive:
  * X amount of shares worth of wstETH
  * Y amount of shares worth of rETH
  * Z amount of shares worth of sfrxETH

* Instead, he receives accordingly to the current adjusted weights, losing rewards occured on his 90% worth of wstETH shares.


## Impact
*  Loss of user's funds.

</br>

## Tools Used
* Manual Review

</br>

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- Short term: N/A
- Long term: The protocol design itself allows the possible scenario for happening. The problem actually, is the same, the user should not be able to receive eth from the derivative which didn't mint some _safEth initially.

issues.title: Reth slippage and fee stealing
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L171-L175


# Vulnerability details

## Impact


The Reth derivative contract calculates the maximum slippage for buying rETH from the Uniswap V3 pool by using the current price in the pool at runtime, without considering the price at which the user submitted the transaction to the mempool:
```
uint rethPerEth = (10 ** 36) / poolPrice();
uint256 minOut = ((((rethPerEth * msg.value) / 10 ** 18) *
    ((10 ** 18 - maxSlippage))) / 10 ** 18);
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L171-L175

Thus, a MEV bot can sandwich the `stake()` transaction, first causing slippage in its favor when the `Reth.deposit()` function is called and secondly earning fees on a price range in the Uniswap V3 pool where the transaction will occur, which the bot already knows in advance. All of this will eat up around 1% of the user's initial deposit:
```
function initialize(address _owner) external initializer {
    _transferOwnership(_owner);
    maxSlippage = (1 * 10 ** 16); // 1%
}
```
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L42-L46

Please note that the slippage occurs relative not to the price at which the user sent the transaction, but to the one chosen by the MEV bot when it decides that it is a favorable time for the bundle.


## Tools Used

x

## Recommended Mitigation Steps


Before submitting a `SafEth.stake()` transaction to the mempool, the user should calculate and manage the slippage. One way to do this is by passing `minOut` as an argument to the `stake()` function.

issues.title: Upgradeability completely breaks decentralization
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L1


# Vulnerability details




## Impact
Owner of SafEth can steal all staked funds.

## Proof of Concept
SafEth is an upgradeable ERC20 contract that handles the conversion between ETH and whatever derivatives that are implemented. But it also has access to the staked funds through the derivatives.
The staked funds are owned by the derivative contracts themselves, but SafEth has privileged access to convert and withdraw these funds to itself. Since SafEth is upgradeable the owner/upgrader of SafEth can upgrade SafEth into a contract from which he can withdraw all staked funds into his own EOA.
Furthermore, the derivatives are also upgradeable, which presents the same issue.

Details of how the staking is done and to which derivatives may very well be centralized, i.e. entrusted to an owner of an upgradeable protocol. But the ownership of the funds themselves must be securely contained in a decentralized fashion, out of reach of any central authority.

The centralizing risk in upgradeability in this case is not like, for example, the upgradeability of a normal ERC20 token. The owner of a token profits from its trading at a value. The value of the protocol resides in its functionality; it doesn't contain any funds itself. If he upgrades it inappropriately his token will instantly lose its value and the owner will lose his business. Any tokens he may have himself will be worthless. Therefore he can be entrusted with the token protocol.
However, in this case, all the value of the protocol is contained in the protocol itself; the protocol owns funds. If the protocol is centrally controlled by an owner, he also owns its value.

Since the protocol is essentially a giant wallet of funds, and that the upgradeability of it gives the owner complete access to these funds, I consider this centralization issue of high severity.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L63-L101
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L170-L185
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L215
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L228-L242


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

An attacker can craft a set of transactions so that when they are depositing funds in the `SafEth` contract, using the `stake()` function, they can understate the value of existing deposits (`preDepositPrice` value), while overstating the value of their deposit (`totalStakeValueEth` value). This vulnerability happens because of how `ethPerDerivative(..)` is calculated for rETH. Specifically, if users cannot deposit directly into the rETH contract, then the `Reth` logic will revert to pricing rETH using the UniswapV3 pool spot price, and also the call to `deposit()` will result in swapping through the same UniswapV3 pool. 

To take advantage of this, an attacker can first decrease the spot price of rETH in the pool, which will result in a lower `preDepositPrice` value when the attacker calls the `stake()` function of the `SafEth` contract. Then, later in the same call when `deposit()` is called for the rETH staking derivative, it will get rETH by swapping ETH -> rETH in the UniswapV3 pool. This swapping will increase the value of the rETH that was received by the swap. The subsequent `ethPerDerivative(..)` function call will then award the attacker an excess amount for their deposit, by overstating the value of the received rETH. This is invalid behavior, as the price of rETH should not be changing atomically in the same transaction.

This is medium severity because an attacker is able to drain significant funds from the `SafEth` contract. However, this can only occur in specific scenarios, based on maxSlippage,

The owner of SafEth can at any time steal all staked funds.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Due to the way in which the `SafEth` share price is calculated, an attacker can front-run the first depositor's transaction and steal funds through an inflation attack. `SafEth::stake` calculates the share price by dividing the total asset amount by the total supply of shares, which is 0 at the time of the first deposit and means that the first depositor will receive 1 share for every wei deposited. The exploit is performed by front-running a large initial deposit and inflating the balance of the staked ether derivative contracts by sending a large number of tokens directly. This causes the `preDepositPrice` to become very large which can result in the victim receiving little/no shares due to rounding given there is no check that the amount to mint is not zero. The result is that the attacker profits at the expense of the victim.

## Proof of Concept
The `preDepositPrice` which is used in calculations of the amount of shares to mint in exchange for a given amount of ether is calculated by:
```
if (totalSupply == 0)
    preDepositPrice = 10 ** 18; // initializes with a price of 1
else preDepositPrice = (10 ** 18 * underlyingValue) / totalSupply;
```

Example exploit steps:
1. Attacker calls `SafEth` with 1 wei for 1 share.
2. Attacker deposits 100 ether worth of staked ether derivative tokens to each derivative token contract in the protocol assuming each has a weight of 1/3.
3. Victim deposits 200 ether for 0 shares due to rounding, assuming a `preDepositPrice` of 300e18 given `totalSupply` of 1e18 and `underlyingValue` of 300e18. Thus, the `mintAmount` calculation is `200e18/300e18` which floor rounds to 0.
4. Attacker withdraws 1 share, profiting 200 ether

# Vulnerability details



## Impact
The first staker can steal the next staked funds.



## Proof of Concept
As the first one to stake, the attacker stakes `minAmount` ETH, for which `minAmount` (or slightly less due to slippage) SafEth tokens are minted.
The attacker immediately unstakes the entire amount except 1 Wei. He now has the total supply of SafEth which is only 1 Wei, and has lost only the small amount of ETH required to cover the slippage.
Now, instead of staking the normal path the attacker simply transfers a large amount `M` of one of the derivative token (e.g. RETH) to the corresponding derivative contract. His 1 Wei SafEth is now worth `M`.

The above attack has the consequence that for the next stake the [`underlyingValue` is `M`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L68-L75) (minus slippage), so [`preDepositPrice = 1e18 * M`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L81), since `totalSupply == 1`. The division causes a rounding error in `totalStakeValueEth` by up to `M`, the amount of which is shared with the attacker's 1 Wei SafEth. This means that the attacker will effectively receive part of the next staker's deposited funds. In the worst case, if `M > totalStakeValueEth`, the second staker will recieve no SafEth and his entire amount staked will be claimable by the attacker.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
To determine the value of sqrtPriceX96 that will cause an overflow, we need to analyze the calculation in the function:

(sqrtPriceX96 * (uint(sqrtPriceX96)) * (1e18)) >> (96 * 2)

The maximum value for a uint256 is 2^256 - 1. An overflow occurs when the result of the multiplication exceeds this value. To find the threshold, we can set up the following inequality:

(sqrtPriceX96^2 * 1e18) / (2^(96*2)) <= 2^256 - 1

Simplifying the inequality:

sqrtPriceX96^2 <= (2^256 - 1) * (2^(96*2)) / 1e18

Taking the square root of both sides to find the threshold for sqrtPriceX96:

sqrtPriceX96 <= sqrt((2^256 - 1) * (2^(96*2)) / 1e18)

After calculating the result, we get:

sqrtPriceX96 <= 5192296858534827

So, any value of sqrtPriceX96 greater than approximately 5,192,296,858,534,827 will result in an overflow.


## Tools Used
calculator

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
use safemath or FullMath library from Uniswap

## Impact
The Asymmetry SafEth protocol aims to help diversify and decentralize liquid staking derivatives, exchanging ether staked in the protocol for staked ether derivative tokens based on some relative weighting. A function exposed by these derivative wrapper contracts, `IDerivative::ethPerDerivative`, takes `uint256 _amount` as argument which is unused in all invocations except for the case when the derivative contract is `Reth`. This is because the rETH deposit pool has a limit above which the balance is capped, currently set to 5000 ether as given by [`RocketDAOProtocolSettingsDeposit::getMaximumDepositPoolSize`](https://etherscan.io/address/0xCc82C913B9f3a207b332d216B101970E39E59DB3#readContract), so any additional rETH is made up by the SafEth protocol through swaps on Uniswap V3.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L108


# Vulnerability details



## Impact
Unstaking is blocked.

## Proof of Concept
When unstaking the `withdraw` of each derivative is called. `Reth.withdraw` withdraws by calling [`RocketTokenRETHInterface(rethAddress()).burn(amount)`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L108). But `RocketTokenRETH.burn` [reverts if the ETH balance is insufficient for the exchange of rETH for ETH](https://etherscan.io/token/0xae78736cd615f374d3085123a210448e74fc6393#code#F6#L140):
```solidity
// Get ETH amount
uint256 ethAmount = getEthValue(_rethAmount);
// Get & check ETH balance
uint256 ethBalance = getTotalCollateral();
require(ethBalance >= ethAmount, "Insufficient ETH balance for exchange");
```
[According to Rocket Pool](https://docs.rocketpool.net/guides/staking/overview.html#the-reth-token) "It's possible that if node operators have put all of the staking pool to work on the Beacon chain, then the liquidity pool won't have enough balance to cover your unstaking. In this scenario, you may find other ways to trade your rETH back to ETH (such as a decentralized exchange like Uniswap (opens new window)) - though they will likely come with a small premium."

In this case `Reth.withdraw` will revert, which blocks the unstaking.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Similarly to when depositing, check if `RocketTokenRETHInterface(rethAddress()).getTotalCollateral() >= RocketTokenRETHInterface(rethAddress()).getEthValue(amount)` and resort to Uniswap if it's not.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the unstake function, the ethAmountToWithdraw variable will always be equal to zero or a negative number, but never a positive number. This is because the ethAmountBefore variable is set to the balance of the contract before any funds are withdrawn from the derivatives, while the ethAmountAfter variable is set to the balance of the contract after the funds have been withdrawn.

Since the function transfers funds to the user, the balance of the contract after the transfer will always be lower than the balance before the transfer, resulting in a negative or zero ethAmountToWithdraw value. Therefore, the equation ethAmountToWithdraw = ethAmountAfter - ethAmountBefore will always result in a zero or negative value.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Fund loss of derivative contracts via flash-loan attacks.

## Proof of Concept
The function `unstake()` is the exit point of the `SafETH.sol` contract. This function burns the users corresponding `SafETH` tokens and pays back the ETH to the users. It gets the `_safEthAmount` from the user and calculates the value of the corresponding asset in ETH and pays to the user. The mechanism is based on the difference of the balance of the contract before and after withdrawing the ETH from the derivative contracts. For a detailed analysis, it's better to look at the 'for-loop' which calculates the amount needed to be withdrawn from each derivative contract:

```
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < derivativeCount; i++) {

                _safEthAmount) / safEthTotalSupply;
            if (derivativeAmount == 0) continue; // if derivative empty ignore
            derivatives[i].withdraw(derivativeAmount);
        }
```
This function is well-written and the loop above guarantees that the user cannot trick the contract and ensures that the user will get his corresponding assets. However, there is a problem with the calculation of the `derivativeAmount` which provides a flash-loan-based attack for an attacker.

issues.title: frxETH price manipulation
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/SfrxEth.sol#L74-L75


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The frxETH derivative uses `price_oracle` of the curve pool which can be used to manipulate the slippage limits

## Proof of Concept

### Background

The `price_oracle()` in the Curve pool is an exponential moving average that exponentially converges from an old value to the last trade value. This is manipulatable in certain conditions. Someone can write a contract that flash-loans a large amount of token A (comparable to the amount of token A in a pool), swaps it for token B in the pool, swap the token B back to token A and repay the flash-loan. This would mean that the last price would significantly differ from the actual price. If there are no transactions on the pool for a while after this, then the pool's `price_oracle()` would converge to a value close to this last price and hence, very different from the actual tokenA/tokenB price.

One key point here is that this kind of price manipulation doesn't require too many funds at risk (since the flashloan is paid up). The maximum loss for the exploiter would just be the fee on the flashloan and the two swaps.

An example of this manipulation for Curve v2 pools can be found in this repo
https://github.com/shuklaayush/brownie-curve-v2

### Vulnerability

- Do a huge flashloan trade for frxETH/ETH pool to crash the frxETH price. Wait for some time for the `price_oracle` to converge to the crashed value
- Any subsequent withdrawal tx will have a low slippage limit for the frxETH -> ETH conversion and can be sandwiched 

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use a proper oracle

The protocol is vulnerable to the well know inflation attack/first deposit bug. The attacker can steal assets from other user's stakes.

The share calculation uses the ERC20 balance of the derivates in the derivates pool. And attacker can transfer ERC20 tokens to inflate the balance. So that underlyingValue&preDepositPrice will be inflated. And the mint amount `mintAmount` will be deflated.

        if (totalSupply == 0)
            preDepositPrice = 10 ** 18; // initializes with a price of 1
        else preDepositPrice = (10 ** 18 * underlyingValue) / totalSupply;

2. Then the attacker does a plain underlying token transfer to the derivate contract, artificially inflating the derivatives[i].balance() value.

the user will become less than 1 and essentially be rounded down to 0 b

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/SfrxEth.sol#L116


# Vulnerability details

## Description
Curve's pool `price_oracle()` returns an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the asset price queried.

According to [investopedia](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/e/ema.asp): An EMA is a type of moving average (MA) that places a greater weight and significance on the most recent data points. Its formula can be summarize in:

$$EMA_{t_{x}} = price_{t_{x}} \times \alpha + EMA_{t_{x-1}} \times (1 - \alpha)$$

where:
* $EMA_{t_{x}}$ is the EMA at time $t_{x}$
* $ price_{t_{x}} $ is the price at time $t_{x}$
* $ EMA_{t_{x-1}} $ is the previous EMA, calculated at time $t_{x-1}$
* $ \alpha $ is a coefficient to indicate the weight of $EMA_{t_{x-1}}$ and $price_{t_{x}}$ in new EMA calculation.

[Curve decided that the contribution of the last oracle price will decrease exponentially with time, controlled by a tunable half life parameter](https://twitter.com/Kurt_M_Barry/status/1404496504581132288). This means that $\alpha = 2^{-\frac{t_{x}-t_{x-1}}{T_{1 / 2}}}$, where $T_{1 / 2}$ is the mentioned tunable half life parameter.

Curve function `price_oracle()` is detailed in [Automatic market-making with dynamic peg (section "Algorithm for repegging"), written to explain Curve pools](https://classic.curve.fi/files/crypto-pools-paper.pdf). The implementation for frxETH/ETH pool is defined as:

```vyper
@external
@view
@nonreentrant('lock')
def price_oracle() -> uint256:
    amp: uint256 = self._A()
    xp: uint256[N_COINS] = self.balances
    D: uint256 = self._get_D(xp, amp)
    return self._ma_price(xp, amp, D)
```

issues.title: Malicious derivative can reenter stake&unstake function
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L113-L120


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If owner private key of one of the derivatives is stolen or the owener behave maliciously, the hacker can upgrade the derivative contract to steal other derivate assets in this protocol.

## Proof of Concept

stake&unstake is not protected by reentrancy guard.

In unstake function, the for loop iterates each derivative to withdraw assets. A malicious derivate will be called in this loop.

The unstake function does not follow the check effect interaction practice. `_burn` is happenning after the withraw iteration.

```
        for (uint256 i = 0; i < derivativeCount; i++) {
            // withdraw a percentage of each asset based on the amount of safETH
            uint256 derivativeAmount = (derivatives[i].balance() *
                _safEthAmount) / safEthTotalSupply;
            if (derivativeAmount == 0) continue; // if derivative empty ignore
            derivatives[i].withdraw(derivativeAmount);    // @audit -------> malicious derivate contract will be called here
        }
        _burn(msg.sender, _safEthAmount);
```

The malicious derivate contract can reenter into unstake&stake function to manipulate attacker's shares and drain assets in other derivates.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- move _burn before the withdraw for loop in unstake.

Or

- add renentrancy guard to stake&unstake.

Internally, we have a price oracle given by an exponential moving average (EMA) applied in N-dimensional price space. Suppose that the last reported price is pLast, and the update happened t seconds ago while the half-time of the EMA
is T1/2. Then the oracle price p_new is given as
```
α = 2^(− t / T1/2);
p_new = pLast * (1 - α) + α * p_old // p_old = current price_oracle
```

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L182-L195


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Once an admin adds a derivative using the `addDerivative()` function, they promptly call the `rebalanceToWeights()` function to rebalance the weights of all derivatives.

During the time between the `addDerivative()` and `rebalanceToWeights()` function calls, referred to as the "golden time," an attacker can execute a transaction that stakes using address B and unstakes using address A (which had previously staked ETH). After front-running, the newly added derivatives are rebalanced. Finally, the attacker calls the unstake function using address B to withdraw the deposited ETH.


## Proof of Concept
Step by step:

1. Attacker uses address A to stake X amount into `SafEth`.

2. Attacker waits for admin calls `addDerivative()` and `rebalanceToWeights()`.

3. Between the function calls, attacker uses address B to stake a very large amount of ETH into the contract to deposit into both old and new derivatives. Immediately after that, the attacker uses address A to unstake their previously staked ETH. At this point, the balances of the derivatives have not been updated, and the attacker will receive more ETH than they are supposed to. Finally, the balances of the new derivatives are rebalanced (too late).

4. Attacker unstake using address B to withdraw the deposited ETH.

yarn, hardhat

The `rebalanceToWeights()` function should be called immediately after adding new derivatives, instead of manually calling it later.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L71-L75


# Vulnerability details

**Likelihood:** Low, because it requires a malicious/compromised owner or upgrade derivative

**Impact:** Critical, because it will break protocol.

## Impact
A successful DoS attack on the `stake()` function due to malicious derivatives would have significant consequences for the protocol. 

## Proof of Concept
Suppose a malicious or compromised `owner` deploys a derivative with gas griefing logic implemented in the `ethPerDerivative()` function and adds it to the protocol derivatives.

Or someone hacked already added derivative admin and upgrade it (if it’s upgradable).

Since `ethPerDerivative()` has gas griefing logic and it is called in the first loop of the `stake()` function, it leads to reverting `stake()` function (DoS).

Transferring ownership to another address would not resolve the issue, as setting the `weight` to zero is insufficient in this situation, and no logic exists to remove the malicious derivative.

Given that this represents the primary entry point of the protocol and could lead to protocol failure, I think this is a high-severity issue.

```solidity
function stake() external payable {
...
        for (uint i = 0; i < derivativeCount; i++)
            underlyingValue +=
                (derivatives[i].ethPerDerivative(derivatives[i].balance()) *
                    derivatives[i].balance()) /
                10 ** 18;
...
}
```
## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider adding `removeDerivative()` function with corresponding logic. And add a role-based access control approach instead of a single admin role.

## Impact
First minter can artificially inflate `preDepositPrice`, enabling him to steal funds from small deposits.

## Proof of Concept
For simplicity consider that wstETH value is equal to ETH and Bob manages to be the first minter on the recently deployed SafEth contract. The attack consist on the following steps.
1. Bob stakes the minimum amount of ETH and receives X safETH tokens
2. Bob unstakes X-1 safETH tokens, leaving `totalSupply() == 1`
3. Bob then directly transfer `10^20` wstETH to the wstEth derivative contact
After this series of actions, the final state of the SafEth contract is `totalSupply() == 1`, `underlyingValue = 1e20`, therefore artificially inflating the `preDepositPrice`. Under these circumstances, any user who attempts to stake a small amount of ETH will have their `mintAmount` rounded down to zero, as shown in the code snippet below

Subsequently, Bob can cash out his stake for a profit. # Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L241


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the Reth.sol derivative contract, if `poolCanDeposit` returns false, then when `ethPerDerivative()` is called, it will use the current value of the UniswapV3 pool instead of the Rocketpool Price. The code checks the current `sqrtPriceX96` from the contract storage, which can be easily manipulated, allowing a malicious user to dilute a staker's received tokens. Knowing ahead of time that the `poolCanDeposit` will return false, can manipulate the price of the pool to make Reth worth significantly more than ETH by buying up all the RETH with a flash loan. Given as the pool only has ~$5M in liquidity and most of the liquidity is concentrated in a small range, this is not very hard to accomplish. issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L246


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Your upgradeable contracts won't be able to unwrap WETH to ETH (tx will revert because gas stipend won't be enough). See more details here: https://forum.openzeppelin.com/t/msg-sender-transfer-runs-out-of-gas-on-a-payable-upgradeable-proxy-contract/3766 . 

## Proof of Concept
The issue lies in the fact that WETH `withdraw` function uses `.transfer()` to transfer ETH, which is only given 2300 fixed gas. This will then invoke `receive` or `fallback` function in the proxy contract, which will then delegate call to the implementation contract (which will cost more gas, and make the 2300 gas insufficient).

This issue is widely known (see  https://forum.openzeppelin.com/t/msg-sender-transfer-runs-out-of-gas-on-a-payable-upgradeable-proxy-contract/3766), and has impacted lots of proxy contracts as well. 

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- The easiest way is for you to extend the existing proxy contract by implementing the `receive` function in the proxy, so when ETH is transferred to the proxy contract, it won't delegate call to the implementation and the gas will be enough. So, your proxy contract will look like:

```
pragma solidity ^0.8.13

import './TransparentUpgradeableProxy.sol';
contract ProxyWithETH is TransparentUpgradeableProxy {
  constructor(...) TransparentUpgradeableProxy(...) {} // call the super constructor

  receive() external payable {}
}
```

issues.title: `withdraw` function in SfrxEth.sol contract is vulnerable to sandwich attack.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/SfrxEth.sol#L74-L82


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Stakers can lose all ETH upon unstaking (on the portion that comes from to frax pool), since the slippage control is incorrectly handled (calculated from spot price).

## Proof of Concept
`withdraw` function in SfrxEth contract is vulnerable to sandwich attack. The pool price is calculated from spot price from Curve pool, which can easily be manipulated. `minOut` variable is also calculated from the manipulatable pool price. So, the potential attack vector is (steps 1,2, & 4 are sandwiched around normal user's transaction):
1. Attacker flashloans ETH out -> deposits to Frax to obtain SfrxETH -> dumps SfrxETH token price
2. Attacker provide enough liquidity (needed just enough liquidity to make sure price doesn't move too much upon swapping)
3. Normal user executes `unstake` which then triggers `withdraw` from SfrxETH -> ETH. But since SfrxETH price is dumped, the obtained ETH is very minimal. The slippage control also easily passes, since the attacker added sufficiently deep liquidity, the price won't move much, so the slippage control check will pass —> this allows the attacker to get to obtain SfrxETH using minimal ETH
4. Attacker unwinds and repays debt. (potentially swapping in other pools e.g. Balancer pool, or just hold onto tokens, since the value will go back to near peg value, so there’s minimal risk).

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- Don't use spot prices. Instead, it's recommended to use oracle service e.g. Chainlink (can contact them to build custom price feed), or use TWAP prices instead.
- Make `unstake` function also accept another slippage control that is computed off-chain. So, it'll be sth like:
```function unstake(uint _safEthAmount, uint _minEthWithdrawAmt) {
  ...
  require(ethAmountToWithdraw >= _minEthWithdrawAmt, 'too few eth');
}
```

Users may receive 0 SafETH in exchange for their deposit if the attacker has inflated the derivatives balances, which leads to the loss of their principal due to rounding off in solidity. 

## Proof of Concept
**Steps to reproduce:**
-- When TotalSupply() of SafEth = 0
      1. Attacker stakes minAmount(0.5 ether) in SafETH. 
      2. Attacker then unstakes all but 1 wei of SafETH. 
      3. Attacker then inflates all of the derivatives by directly transferring Z amounts of the respective underlyings (reth, sFRXEth, wStETH in our case) to the **respective derivatives address**. Thus increasing the balances of all the respective derivatives. 
4. Now 1 wei of SafETH is equivalent to Z amount of underlying staked derivatives, thus increasing the `preDepositPrice` in the stake function. 
5. Now if users stake less than Z amount, they will be minted 0 SafETH due to rounding off, while their deposited ETH will be lost to the attacker. 
6. Attacker won't have any issues making Z amount as big as possible since 1 wei of SafEth is owned by him. 

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
- Uniswap V2 solved this problem by sending the first 1000 LP tokens to the zero address. The same can be done in this case, i.e. when totalSupply() == 0, send the first SafETH to the zero address to enable share dilution.
- In `stake()`, ensure the number of shares to be minted is non-zero:
require(mintAmount != 0, "No shares minted");

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L171-L183


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Stakers can lose all ETH (obtaining minimal rETH back) upon staking (on the portion that goes to rocket pool), since the slippage control is incorrectly handled (calculated from spot price).

## Proof of Concept
`deposit` function in rETH contract is vulnerable to sandwich attack. The pool price is calculated from spot price, which can easily be manipulated. `minOut` is also calculated from the manipulatable price. So, the potential attack vector is: 1. Attacker flashloans out ETH and dumps ETH price 2. Attacker provide deep enough liquidity around the dumped ETH price 3. Normal user executes swap from ETH -> rETH. Since ETH price is dumped, the obtained rETH is very minimal. The slippage control also easily passes, since the attacked added deep liquidity around the manipulated price, so the price didn’t move much. —> this allows attacker to get to buy ETH using rETH at a very very low price 4. Attacker unwinds and repays debt. (potentially swapping in other pools e.g. Curve, or just hold onto tokens, since the value will go back to near peg value, so there’s minimal risk). 

The attacker vector itself should be clear enough to show that there’s a vulnerability here, so I don’t think an actual PoC code is needed here. Let me know otherwise tho.

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
- Don't use spot prices. Instead, it's recommended to use oracle service e.g. Chainlink (https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/price-feeds/addresses), or use TWAP prices instead.
- Make `stake` function also accept another slippage control that is computed off-chain (preventing flashloan attempts). So, it'll be sth like:
```function stake(uint _minRethAmt) {
  ...
  require(_minRethAmt >= mintAmount, 'too few reth');
}
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

When a user calls `stake` it sends `msg.value` with the amount of ETH desired to be staked. Firstly, the underlying value of each derivative is calculated in a `for` loop.

```solidity
        // Getting underlying value in terms of ETH for each derivative
        for (uint i = 0; i < derivativeCount; i++)
            underlyingValue +=
                (derivatives[i].ethPerDerivative(derivatives[i].balance()) *
                    derivatives[i].balance()) /
                10 ** 18;
```

The problem is that the `ethPerDerivative` function is called and the whole balance of the derivative is passed as argument. This means, that value returned in ETH is for the whole balance. However, this value is multiplied by the balance of the derivatives again which makes the calculation wrong. For example, if the balance of `rEth` is 5 tokens (each valued at 1 ETH for simplicity), the calculation will look like this:

`underlyingValue += 5 ETH * 5 (tokens) / 10 ** 18;` and it will return 25 ETH as `underlyingValue`.

This is then used to calculate the `preDepositPrice`, which is used to calculate the `mintAmount` at the end. Basically, all of the calculations will be wrong.

2. After the last loop the `underlyingValue = 75 ETH` which will be used for the rest of the calculations while the correct amount should be 25.

```

## Impact
In stake function we calculation mintAmount by "totalStakeValueEth * 10 ** 18) / preDepositPrice" where totalStakeValueEth is ether staked by user and preDepositPrice is calculated by "(10 ** 18 * underlyingValue) / totalSupply" where underlyingValue is previously staked ether. If simplify it we will have mintAmount equal to "totalSupply*totalStakeValueEth/underlyingValue".  

Now first use can stake minimum eth which will be "totalWeight/weight+1" and weight will be higher from all. ````

2.When second user come then first user can front-run him by directly transfer more worth of staked in protocols to directly to Reth.sol, SfrxEth.sol and WstEth.sol.
3.First user will transfer more worth of staked eth to make underlyingValue greater than totalSupply*totalStakeValueEth(value staked by second user).
4.In this way upcoming users will have zero mintAmount because denominator will be greater than numerator.
````

Solidity visual developer

My recommendation step is that when mintAmount will be zero then stake function should revert.

* In [SafEth.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol) there is a function `stake()` which provides an opportunity for users to distribute their ETH between multiple pre-defined derivatives.     IStEthEthPool(LIDO_CRV_POOL).exchange(1, 0, stEthBal, minOut);
```

The exact implementation is to get stETH price from the curve pool used in withdraw.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

Get ETH value the curve pool. We can use `get_dy` method of the pool.

issues.title: `Reth.ethPerDerivative()` is wrongly implemented
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L211-L216


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`Reth.ethPerDerivative()` is used to calculate `underlyingVaule` and `totalStakeValueEth` in `SafEth.stake()` and these values would be calculated wrongly because `Reth.ethPerDerivative()` returns the wrong value.

## Proof of Concept
`Reth.ethPerDerivative()` should return the price of rETH in terms of ETH.

```solidity
    function ethPerDerivative(uint256 _amount) public view returns (uint256) {
        if (poolCanDeposit(_amount))
            return
                RocketTokenRETHInterface(rethAddress()).getEthValue(10 ** 18);
        else return (poolPrice() * 10 ** 18) / (10 ** 18);
    }
```

In this function, the `_amount` param means the amount of rETH but it calls `poolCanDeposit()` with this param.

But `poolCanDeposit(uint256 _amount)` checks if the `_amount` of ETH can be deposited to the rETH pool by validating min/max limits.

For now, `poolCanDeposit()` is called with the amount of rETH instead of ETH, furthermore, it doesn't make sense to check if the rETH can be deposited to the pool again.

So it's incorrect to call `poolCanDeposit()` with the amount of rETH and it will output the different price using `poolPirce()` in case `poolCanDeposit()` returns false.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
I think `ethPerDerivative()` shouldn't call `poolCanDeposit()`.

```solidity
    function ethPerDerivative(uint256 _amount) public view returns (uint256) {
        return RocketTokenRETHInterface(rethAddress()).getEthValue(10 ** 18);
    }
```

issues.title: Wrong slippage in withdraw() of WstEth can cause DOS Or LOSS of user funds due to front-running depending on difference between dy and minOut.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/WstEth.sol#L60


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The 'withdraw' function has a parameter called 'minOut', which is calculated by subtracting the maximum slippage percentage from the stEthBal. However, stEthBal represents the token amount of 'x' that we have, whereas we are actually exchanging it for token 'y'. This is a bug because we are passing the amount of token 'x', but we should be passing the amount of token 'y' instead. This mistake can cause a Denial of Service (DOS) if minOut is less than 'dy', and it can give an opportunity for an attacker to use front-running for instant profit if minOut is much higher than 'dy'.

## Proof of Concept
We are calculating amount of minOut by using 
````
uint256 minOut = (stEthBal * (10 ** 18 - maxSlippage)) / 10 ** 18;
````
Since stEthBal represents the amount of token 'x' (stEth) and we are exchanging it for token 'y' (ETH), we should pass the amount of 'y' instead of 'x'.

## Tools Used
Solidity visual developer

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
My recommendation is use get_dy to get amount of y tokens and subtract maximum slippage percentage from it like
````
uint256 minOut = (get_dy(1, 0, stEthBal) * (10 ** 18 - maxSlippage)) / 10 ** 18;
````

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L63


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

First staker can inflate the rate of minting SafEth token per deposited ETH, leading to the loss of next stakers funds.

It's a well-known attack vector, explained for example [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-rubicon-findings/issues/397).

## Proof of Concept

Next scenario possible:
1. Attacker stake 1 wei of ETH on newly deployed SafETH.sol contract, minting 1 wei of `SafETH` token.
2. Attacker sends 1 WST_ETH token to `WstETH` derivative address.
3. Next user stake 0.5 ETH, but since the current `underlyingValue` is 1 ETH (from WST_ETH sent by the attacker) and `totalSupply` of SafETH is 1 wei - `preDepositPrice` is overinflated and user mints 0 wei of SafETH, while the attacker could withdraw all staked 1.5 ETH.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider adding a restriction to mint more than 0 wei of SafETH token on ```stake()``` function call or sending the first 1000 wei of token to a zero address.

issues.title: Reentrancy attacks
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/SfrxEth.sol#L84


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This line of code is used to send ETH to the msg.sender (which is expected to be the owner of the contract) after exchanging FRX_ETH tokens for ETH on the FRX_ETH_CRV_POOL_ADDRESS Curve pool. However, using call to send ETH can be dangerous, as it opens the contract up to reentrancy attacks. If an attacker can trigger the call function to be executed again during the execution of this function, they could potentially drain the contract's ETH balance.As there is no validation code and limit of ether amount. 

## Proof of Concept
One notable example of reentrancy attacks in the past. One famous example is the DAO hack, which occurred in 2016 and resulted in the theft of millions of dollars worth of Ether. In this attack, an attacker was able to exploit a vulnerability in the DAO smart contract that allowed them to repeatedly call a function in the contract before the previous call had finished executing, thereby draining the contract's funds.


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To prevent these types of vulnerabilities, it's important to follow best practices for using call(). This includes properly validating input parameters, using the require() and assert() statements to check for conditions before executing the call, and limiting the amount of gas that can be used by the call. Additionally, using more modern and secure alternatives to call(), such as transfer() or send(), can help mitigate these risks. Additionally, it may be a good idea to limit the amount of ETH that can be withdrawn at once to further reduce the potential impact of a reentrancy attack.

To stake ETH into safETH, one should call `SafEth.stake()` method. The calculation of preDepositPrice is done like this:
1. For the first staking, the price is 1

```

Please note that the underlyingValue is the total value in ETH of all derivatives.
Each derivative's underlyingValue is calculated as follows:
```solidity
underlyingValue += (derivatives[i].ethPerDerivative(derivatives[i].balance()) *
                    derivatives[i].balance()) /
                10 ** 18;
```

And the derivative balance is calculated as follows (an example for WST_ETH):
```solidity
function balance() public view returns (uint256) {

}

Each derivative has a function `ethPerDerivative`, which returns the eth price of the derivative.

Manual review

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L240

## Impact
`poolPrice` is used to calculate the price of `reth` in terms of `eth`. To do this, the function is calling `slot0` on UniswapV3 Pool. `slot0` captures the most recent token balance and hence can be easily manipulated. 

As per [Uniswap V3 docs](https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v3/reference/core/interfaces/pool/IUniswapV3PoolState#slot0), `slot0` stores the current tick of the pool. Since it is only a single tick, price can be easily manipulated by creating instantaneous token imbalances in the pool. 


## Proof of Concept
`deposit` function calculates the `minOut` parameter (minimum `rEth` while swapping for `WETH`) using the `poolPrice`. If `poolPrice` is momentarily inflated by manipulating latest tick of Uniswap pool, `minOut` can be significantly low. This can potentially cause a large slippage while swapping WETH to reth causing a loss to depositors.

```

 function deposit() external payable onlyOwner returns (uint256) {
   ...
        if (!poolCanDeposit(msg.value)) {
            uint rethPerEth = (10 ** 36) / poolPrice(); //@audit -> price uses slot0 - can be manipulated

            uint256 minOut = ((((rethPerEth * msg.value) / 10 ** 18) *
                ((10 ** 18 - maxSlippage))) / 10 ** 18); 

            IWETH(W_ETH_ADDRESS).deposit{value: msg.value}();
            uint256 amountSwapped = swapExactInputSingleHop(
                W_ETH_ADDRESS,
                rethAddress(),
                500,
                msg.value,
                minOut
            );

            return amountSwapped;
        }
   ...
}

```

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use TWAP price instead of `slot0` price in `poolPrice` function

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/WstEth.sol#L57


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In the Line 57, the unwrap function call is made without checking the return value in the withdraw function. The unwrap function is used to convert wrapped stETH tokens into stETH tokens, which can then be exchanged for ETH. If the unwrap function call fails, the contract will continue to execute and try to send ETH to the owner, resulting in a loss of funds. This is because the unwrap function will return an error if the contract doesn't have enough wrapped stETH tokens to convert, or if the conversion itself fails for some reason.

## Proof of Concept
This vulnerability could involve deliberately calling the withdraw function with an amount of wrapped stETH tokens that exceeds the amount that the contract actually holds. This would trigger the contract to attempt to unwrap more tokens than it actually has, causing the unwrap function to fail and return a value of false. However, because the contract doesn't check the return value of unwrap, it will still proceed with the exchange and attempt to send ETH to the owner. As a result, the contract will lose the funds that it attempted to send, since the unwrap function failed and didn't actually release any stETH tokens. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by calling the withdraw function with a large amount of wrapped stETH tokens, causing the contract to lose a significant amount of funds.


## Tools Used
Remix
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To prevent such a loss of funds, the contract should check the return value of the unwrap function and revert the transaction if the function call fails. This can be done using an if statement or a require statement, which will check if the function call returned a success value or not.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

`poolPrice()` in Reth.sol uses the Uniswap pool spot price as an oracle. This makes it vulnerable to manipulation from flash loans.

## Proof of Concept

The `Reth.poolprice()` function should return the expected exchange rate between rETH and ETH. But the return value can be manipulated because it is using the [spot price of the Uniswap pool](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L241). The liquidity of this pool is only $5 million, so flashloans that frontrun a `SafEth.stake()` call can easily alter the spot price of the pool. The [`minAmount` value calculated by Reth](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L173-L174) relies on the spot price too, so it does not help prevent the protocol from swapping to rETH at a very bad rate that is manipulated by frontrunning.

## Tools Used

Manual analysis

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

[Do not use Uniswap pool spot price for a price oracle](https://shouldiusespotpriceasmyoracle.com/). Instead, use Chainlink or another source of price data that cannot easily be manipulated.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A malicious attacker can use this vulnerability to withdraw more ETH than they are entitled to or to cause a denial-of-service (DoS) attack, resulting in the loss of user funds or the inability to withdraw funds.

## Proof of Concept
Consider the following scenario. Suppose a malicious actor has a contract that can receive ETH and execute a fallback function, then, the malicious actor could perform the following steps:


*. Call the `withdraw` function of the `SfrxEth` contract and supply a large value for the `_amount` parameter.
The `SfrxEth` contract calls the redeem function of the `IsFrxEth` contract, which transfers `_amount` of the `SfrxEth` token to the `SfrxEth` contract.

*. The SfrxEth contract obtains the balance of `FRX_ETH_ADDRESS` token it holds.

*. The SfrxEth contract approves the `FRX_ETH_CRV_POOL_ADDRESS to spend FRX_ETH_ADDRESS` token of the balance it holds.

*. The `SfrxEth` contract calls the exchange function of the `FRX_ETH_CRV_POOL_ADDRESS`, which converts the `FRX_ETH_ADDRESS` token to ETH and sends the ETH to the SfrxEth contract.

*. The `SfrxEth` contract calls `msg.sender.call{value: address(this).balance}("")` to send the ETH to the `msg.sender`.


However, if the malicious actor's contract has a fallback function that can call back into the `SfrxEth` contract, the malicious actor can execute a reentrancy attack.

The malicious actor's contract can call the `withdraw` function again before the `msg.sender.call{value: address(this).balance}("")` call completes.

The malicious actor's contract can then execute some malicious code before the first `withdraw` call completes, causing a loss of funds or disrupting the normal operation of the `SfrxEth` contract.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L84-L86

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L140-L143


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
There is no way to remove a derivative from the ```derivatives``` mapping. Although it is possible to set the weight to 0, the loops still make the number of iterations equal to ```derivativeCount``` (```derivativeCount``` cannot be decreased). # Vulnerability details

## Impact
In all contracts within scope, the receive() function is implemented without any access controls or restrictions, allowing anyone to send Ether directly to the contract without going through the intended staking process.

The current receive() function implementation:

`receive() external payable {}`

This could lead to potential security risks, such as bypassing the staking functionality and causing an incorrect representation of the staked Ether in the contract. Additionally, it might lead to difficulties in tracking the origin of the funds and managing the contract's balance.

## Proof of Concept
N/A

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To mitigate potential risks associated with the unsecure use of the receive() function, it is recommended to remove the function entirely and ensure that the only way to send Ether to the contract is through the intended stake() function.

If there is a legitimate need for the contract to accept Ether directly, consider implementing access controls and restrictions to limit the sender addresses and the amount of Ether that can be sent directly to the contract. In such a case, it is crucial to ensure that the received Ether is appropriately managed and does not interfere with the contract's primary functionalities.

By removing or securing the receive() function, you can prevent the contract from receiving Ether from unintended sources and ensure that the contract's balance and staking functionality are not compromised.

issues.title: SfrxETH.ethPerDerivative returns a wrong value other than the price denominated in ETH
Derivate `WstEth` contract incorrectly calculates the price of the `ETH`
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/WstEth.sol#L87


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `WstEth` contract incorrectly calculates the price of ETH in terms of WstETH.

The function returns the price of WstETH in terms of stETH. The underlying asset which we desire is ETH.

Since stETH does not have the same value as ETH the output price is incorrect.

The impact is severe as `underlyingValue` and `totalStakeValueEth` through the `stake()` function in the `SafEth.sol` contract [SafEth.sol#L63](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L63) are wrong calculated. 


## Proof of Concept
The function `IWstETH(token).getStETHByWstETH()` only converts WstETH to stETH. Thus, `ethPerDerivative()` returns the value of WstETH in terms of stETH. Also, the `@notice` comment in the code says that the derivate's price should be in terms of ETH.
```solidity
    /**
        @notice - Get price of derivative in terms of ETH
     */
    function ethPerDerivative(uint256 _amount) public view returns (uint256) {
        return IWStETH(WST_ETH).getStETHByWstETH(10 ** 18);
    }
```


## Tools Used
Manuel review
https://code4rena.com/reports/2022-05-alchemix/#m-15-lido-adapter-incorrectly-calculates-the-price-of-the-underlying-token


## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add extra steps to `ethPerDerivative()` to approximate the rate for converting stETH to ETH. This can be done using the same curve pool that is used to convert stETH to ETH in `withdraw()`.

# Vulnerability details

# [M-01] Out-of-work derivatives or adding invalid derivatives will make the entire project inaccessible and unrecoverable.

## Impact
Out-of-work derivatives or incorrectly calling of `addDerivative` could lead to the user losing funds, the project will be inaccessible and unrecoverable forever.

## Proof of Concept
In the `SafEth` contract , we have 2 key external functions `addDerivative` and `rebalanceToWeights` for the owner, and also 2 external functions `stake` and `unstake` for the user. At the meanwhile, the `SafEth` contract is the only owner of these derivatives (now we have `Reth`, `SfrxEth` and `WstEth`). Only the `SafEth` can call the `deposit`, `withdraw` and `setMaxSlippage` of these derivatives.

The owner can add new derivatives, but can not update the derivative address corresponding to one index. If one derivative is out-of-work or the owner adds an invalid derivative by `addDerivative` into the project, all the future calls of `rebalanceToWeights`, `stake` and `unstake` will revert. The user will lose funds and no one can recovery.

Invalid derivatives could be:
1. A derivative whos owner is not `SafEth`

issues.title: User can experience unnecessary slippage due to miscalculation in `ethPerDerivative` and `poolCanDeposit` when staking Reth
Unstake() and rebalanceToWeights() at the SafEth.sol contract can get DoSed
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L131


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `unstake()` and `rebalanceToWeights()` functions iterate over the `derivatives` mapping and call the `withdraw()` function on them. 

The `withdraw()` function on the `Reth.sol` contract is the following:

```
function withdraw(uint256 amount) external onlyOwner {
  RocketTokenRETHInterface(rethAddress()).burn(amount);
  // solhint-disable-next-line
  (bool sent, ) = address(msg.sender).call{value: address(this).balance}("");
  require(sent, "Failed to send Ether");
}
```

It tries to convert rETH back to ETH directly with RocketPool. In case is not possible to do the convertion the execution will revert, causing a DoS on the functions `unstake()` and `rebalanceToWeights()`.

## Proof of Concept

The [Rocket Pool Docs](https://docs.rocketpool.net/guides/staking/overview.html#the-reth-token) docs have the following note:

"Trading rETH back for ETH directly with Rocket Pool is only possible when the staking pool has enough ETH in it to handle your trade.

It's possible that if node operators have put all of the staking pool to work on the Beacon chain, then the liquidity pool won't have enough balance to cover your unstaking. In this scenario, you may find other ways to trade your rETH back to ETH (such as a decentralized exchange like Uniswap (opens new window)) - though they will likely come with a small premium."

Also this can be read directly from the Rocket Pool contracts starting at the [burn](https://github.com/rocket-pool/rocketpool/blob/967e4d3c32721a84694921751920af313d1467af/contracts/contract/token/RocketTokenRETH.sol#L106) function

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Don't rely only on trading rETH back for ETH directly with Rocket Pool, when this is no possible, use an AMM like Uniswap or Balancer

## Impact

The `WstEth` contract implements the ETH derivative for the Lido protocol. The stETH token is the liquid representation of the ETH staked in this protocol.

There are two different places in the codebase that indicate that the implementation is assuming a peg of 1 ETH ~= 1 stETH, each with different consequences. Even though both tokens have a tendency to keep the peg, this hasn't been always the case as it can be seen in [this charth](https://nomics.com/exchanges/curve-curve-finance-ethereum/markets/0xae7ab96520de3a18e5e111b5eaab095312d7fe84-0xeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeeee) or [this dashboard](https://dune.com/LidoAnalytical/Curve-ETHstETH). This function is intended to work as an estimation of the current value in ETH of one unit (1e18) of the underlying asset. In this implementation, the function simply queries the amount of stETH for one unit (1e18) of wstETH and returns that value, which clearly indicates a conversion rate of 1 stETH = 1 ETH.

## Impact

The `stake` function present in the `SafEth` contract accepts user deposits and stakes them into the different derivatives. To calculate the user shares in the vault, the function will first calculate the total ETH value for all the current staked assets and then it will calculate how much ETH resulted after splitting by weight the deposit into the different derivatives. Both of these calculations use the `ethPerDerivative` function of each derivative.

To calculate the total value in ETH for the current staked assets (`underlyingValue`), the implementation will loop each derivative and multiply its balance by the result of `ethPerDerivative` (that returns the current ETH value for one unit, 1e18, of the derivative asset). # Vulnerability details

## Impact
When staking the amount of minted SafETH may not reflect the share of the unstakeable Ether. Depending on the blockchain state staking and immediate unstaking may cause a loss or gain of ETH at the expense of the SafETH holders.

## Proof of Concept

In https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L73 the currently unstakeable Ether is calculated as `derivative.ethPerDerivative(derivative.balance()) * derivative.balance()`. issues.title: Slippage protection in `Reth.deposit()` does not work
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L171


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
in [`Reth.deposit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L171) the spot price of the UniV3 pool is used to compute the `minOut` amount. This is a problem because the user cannot know in advance what `minOut` will be since the spot price can change from the moment the staking tx is sent to the moment it is included, and can be lower than expected. This also makes the staking vulnerable to sandwich attacks.

## Proof of Concept
1. Alice stakes 30 ETH, assuming that weights are equal, 10 ETH will be deposited into RETH
2. Assume the price of RETH is 1 ETH at the moment Alice sends the tx
3. Other tx are included before and those change the spot price of RETH on the UniV3 pool to 1.01 ETH
4. In `Reth.deposit()`, if `poolCanDeposit(msg.value)` is false, then `rethPerEth` = 1/1.01 = 0.99 and `minout` = 0.99 * (1 - 0.01) * msg.value = 0.99 * 0.99 * 10 = 9.8.
5. `minOut` = 9.8, so slippage allowed is 2% instead of 1%

The slippage protection does not work, since the minimum price accepted is 1% less than the spot price at tx execution, which can change before the tx is executed.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
For `rethPerEth` use the UniV3 oracle price instead of the spot price.

## Impact
An attacker can exploit it to mint an excessive amount of `safETH` tokens and cause inflation, this could lead to a loss of value for users who hold `safETH` tokens and can harm the reputation of the contract.

## Description
The `mintAmount` calculation in the stake function has an integer overflow vulnerability.
This vulnerability can allow an attacker to mint an excessive amount of `safETH` tokens and cause inflation, the vulnerability is due to the use of the multiplication of the `totalStakeValueEth` with `10^18` and then dividing it by `preDepositPrice` to calculate the `mintAmount`, If `totalStakeValueEth` is very large, the multiplication can cause an integer overflow vulnerability.

## Proof of Concept
I can confirm that the `mintAmount` calculation in the stake function has an integer overflow vulnerability.

The following line of code in the stake function calculates the `mintAmount` by multiplying the `totalStakeValueEth` with `10^18` and then dividing it by `preDepositPrice`:
```solidity
uint256 mintAmount = (totalStakeValueEth * 10 ** 18) / preDepositPrice;
```
Since `totalStakeValueEth` can be very large, the multiplication can cause an integer overflow vulnerability, an attacker can exploit it to mint an excessive amount of `safETH` tokens and cause inflation.

## Tools Used

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider modifying the code to check for potential integer overflow vulnerabilities and take necessary precautions, such as using SafeMath library, to prevent such vulnerabilities.

```solidity
uint256 mintAmount = SafeMath.div(SafeMath.mul(totalStakeValueEth, 10 ** 18), preDepositPrice);
```
This will prevent integer overflow vulnerabilities in the calculation of `mintAmount`.

uint256 totalSupply = totalSupply();
uint256 preDepositPrice; // Price of safETH in regards to ETH

The impact of this vulnerability could result in an incorrect price of `safETH` in terms of ETH, which may lead to losses for users.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The stake() function in the smart contract is vulnerable to front running attacks, which can result in a loss of funds for stakers.

## Proof of Concept
A front running attack can occur when a malicious user monitors the Ethereum mempool for incoming transactions, and if they see a large transaction to the stake() function, they can quickly submit their own transaction with a higher gas price to be included before the original transaction. This allows the attacker to manipulate the price of the derivatives before the original transaction is processed, resulting in the original transaction receiving a worse rate than anticipated.

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
To mitigate this issue, it is recommended to add an optional parameter to the stake() function that allows the staker to specify a minimum amount of safETH tokens to be minted. This would ensure that stakers receive a minimum number of tokens regardless of any price manipulation by attackers.

issues.title: Purchase of RETH on Uniswap can be sandwich attacked
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L240


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The attacker can perform a sandwich attack and enforce an arbitrary RETH purchase rate when the user `deposit`s when `stake` or `rebalanceToWeights` are called.

## Proof of Concept

For the attack to work SafETH derivative for RETH must be in the mode of buying on Uniswap (`poolCanDeposit(amt) == false`). With sufficient capital the attacker can impose an arbitrary price of RETH on Uniswap by performing a sandwich attack.

- The attacker buys as much RETH for ETH on Uniswap as possible inflating RETH price.
- In the next transaction, the user then runs `deposit` on RETH derivative which buys very little RETH for a lot of ETH inflating RETH price even more.
- In the next transaction, the attacker sells RETH for more ETH than they put in initially effectively earning the user's loss.

This is possible because when the RETH derivative buys RETH, it calculates the maximum slippage based on the current price of RETH with no consideration for the historical rates. 

## Tools Used

Manual review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

In function `poolPrice` use the Uniswap's `observe` mechanism to get the rate more difficult. Uniswap provides a library with the helpers to make it easier with `consult` and `getQuoteAtTick`: https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-periphery/blob/main/contracts/libraries/OracleLibrary.sol

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The function `Unstake() of SafEth.sol` is lacking a reentrancy guard, meaning this can allow a malicious actor to easily reenter into the function and drain all of the funds from the derivatives. 
HERE IS THE ATTACK FLOW:
1. The attacker calls the function `Unstake()` with _safEthAmount to unstake
2. The contract does the necessary logic then calls msg.sender with an  `ethAmountToWithdraw` value
3. The attacker then hooks the call and recalls back into the function.

This can go on until the derivatives balances are completely wiped

Note that, with the current implementation, an attacker can instead call the `Unstake() function` with _safEthAmount equal to the balance of all of the derivatives and all of the eth from the contracts will be converted and deposited into the safEth contract which will then be sent to msg.sender

issues.title: First staker can steal deposits from other stakers
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L81


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
in [`SafeEth.stake()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L63) the `totalSupply` can be manipulated by the first staker to be a very low value, which allows him to steal the deposits of successive stakers.

## Proof of Concept
1. First staker stakes 0.5 ETH, receives `x` SafETH. TotalSupply will be `x` after staking.
2. Unstake `x` SafETH - 1 wei, so that the totalSupply goes down to 1 wei.
3. Send 10 WstETH to the WstEth contract

Another second staker comes and:
1. Stake 5 ETH: `underlyingValue` = 1e19 (from the WstETh sent directly by first staker), `totalSupply` is not 0, so `preDepositPrice` = 1e18 * 1e19 / 1 = 1e19 * 1e18
2. `totalStakeValue` will be around the amount staked,say 5*1e18.
3. `mintAmount` = 5 * 1e18 * 1e18 / (1e19 * 1e18) = 0
4. Second staker does not receive any SafETH

Then the first staker:
1. withdraws the 1 wei of SafETH he still holds, and gets the ETH value of 10 + 5 WstETH, stealing 5 ETH from the second staker.

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Send a fraction of the shares minted during the first mint (when totalSupply == 0) to an owner controlled account to assure a minimum value to the totalSupply, and avoid the totalSupply to be manipulated to 1 wei by the first staker.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/WstEth.sol#L86-L88


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In [`WstEth.ethPerDerivative()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/44b5cd94ebedc187a08884a7f685e950e987261c/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/WstEth.sol#L86) the value returned is `IWStETH(WST_ETH).getStETHByWstETH(10 ** 18);`, which is the price in stETH of 1 WstETH, while it should return the price in ETH instead. This will return an incorrect `mintAmount` during staking.

## Proof of Concept
Let's say the weights are (WstETH = 0.8, SfrxETH = 0.1, RETH = 0.1), and for simplicity WstETH, SfrxETH and RETH have all the same price and equal to 1 ETH, but StETH has the price of 0.998 ETH.
1. First user deposits 100 ETH
   1. totalSupply == 0 so preDepositPrice = 10 ** 18
   2. Neglecting fees and slippage, values for `depositAmount` for the 3 derivatives are all equal to 1
   3. `derivativeReceivedEthValue` will also be always 1 except for WstETH for wich it will be 1.002 because `WstEth.ethPerDerivative()` has the bug and returns the amount of StETH instead of the amount of ETh per WstETH.
   4. totalStakeValueEth = 3.002 instead of 3 as expected
   5. mintAmount = 3.002 SafETH instead of 3 as expected

## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add a function `StETHOraclePrice()` that takes the chainlink oracle to get stETH/ETH price and calculate the actual price in ETH as follows

```diff

    function ethPerDerivative(uint256 _amount) public view returns (uint256) {
-       return IWStETH(WST_ETH).getStETHByWstETH(10 ** 18);
+       return StETHOraclePrice() * IWStETH(WST_ETH).getStETHByWstETH(10 ** 18);
    }

```

issues.title: Sandwich Attack on `swapExactInputSingleHop` function
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/tree/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L83-L102


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
While interacting with Uniswap, current contracts do not define a significant `_minOut` making them susceptible to "Sandwich attacks" When the `swapExactInputSingleHop` function is executed, an attacker may exploit a substantial token swap amount by paying more Gas to prioritize their transaction. By buying or selling on Uniswap, the attacker can manipulate the token price, causing the existing contract to complete the transaction at a lower token price. This attack method siphons a minor percentage of tokens from every `swapExactInputSingleHop` operation.

Consequently, impacted functions may revert, potentially leading to losses.

## Proof of Concept

See: https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/tree/main/contracts/SafEth/derivatives/Reth.sol#L83-L102

```
function swapExactInputSingleHop(
        address _tokenIn,
        address _tokenOut,
        uint24 _poolFee,
        uint256 _amountIn,
        uint256 _minOut
    ) private returns (uint256 amountOut) {
        IERC20(_tokenIn).approve(UNISWAP_ROUTER, _amountIn);
        ISwapRouter.ExactInputSingleParams memory params = ISwapRouter
            .ExactInputSingleParams({
                tokenIn: _tokenIn,
                tokenOut: _tokenOut,
                fee: _poolFee,
                recipient: address(this),
                amountIn: _amountIn,
                amountOutMinimum: _minOut,
                sqrtPriceLimitX96: 0
            });
        amountOut = ISwapRouter(UNISWAP_ROUTER).exactInputSingle(params);
    }
```

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
An attacker can frontrun the first deposit on the safETH contract. By exploiting a donation attack an attacker can set the price of safETH very high. Because of division rounding the user will then receive less safETH than normal. The attacker can then withdraw his safETH for all (or a portion) of funds in the contract. Thus stealing (a part of) the users deposit.

Assume only 1 derivative exists (wstETH):

Assuming 1:1 peg between stETH and ETH may skew calculations when calculating underlying Value.

## Proof of Concept

When calculating ETH per derivative, 1e18 is used, instead of the `_amount` parameter (which is fine, but that means `_amount` is obsolete). For example, in WstEth.sol, the function ethPerDerivative wants to know the conversion rate between WstEth and stEth. (about 1.1165:1 currently). The protocol then assumes that stEth and Eth (0.99:1) is 1:1.

```
    function ethPerDerivative(uint256 _amount) public view returns (uint256) {
        return IWStETH(WST_ETH).getStETHByWstETH(10 ** 18);
    }
```

In SafEth.sol, the comment states that `underlyingValue` is in terms of ETH for each derivative, but for the case of stETH, stETH is assumed to be 1:1 with ETH.

```
        // Getting underlying value in terms of ETH for each derivative
        for (uint i = 0; i < derivativeCount; i++)
            underlyingValue +=
                (derivatives[i].ethPerDerivative(derivatives[i].balance()) *
                    derivatives[i].balance()) /
                10 ** 18;
```
UnderlyingValue calculation: 
underlyingValue += (derivatives[i].ethPerDerivative(derivatives[i].balance()) * derivatives[i].balance()) / 10 ** 18;

Assuming balance in WstEth.sol is 100WstEth, and conversion between WstETH and stETH is 1.1165:1
Since ethPerDerivative does not input the derivatives[i].balance() but 1e18 instead, 
underlyingValue += (1.1165e18 * 100e18 / 1e18) = 1.1165e20 (stETH value, which is assumed to be 1:1) 
The actual total ETH value in WstEth.sol is supposedly 1.1165e20 (stETH) * 0.99 (rate between stETH and ETH) = 1.105335e20

Also, stETH value is also known to depeg from ETH sometimes.

## Impact
There can be an abuse of the deposit function in the SfrxEth contract to deposit an arbitrary amount of ETH, causing a denial-of-service attack by consuming all the gas available in the contract. 

## Proof of Concept
The deposit function has no validation for the `msg.value` parameter, which allows an attacker to deposit an arbitrary amount of ETH resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) attack.

The relevant code is in the deposit() function:
```solidity
function deposit() external payable onlyOwner returns (uint256) {
    ...
    frxETHMinterContract.submitAndDeposit{value: msg.value}(address(this));
    ...
}

The `msg.value` parameter is passed directly to the `submitAndDeposit` function of the "frxETHMinterContract", which is an external contract, this function does not validate the input, which means an attacker can call the `deposit()` function with an arbitrary amount of ETH.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Consider adding input validation in the `deposit()` function to ensure that the `msg.value` parameter is within acceptable bounds.

as well as the Reth.sol#L228.poolPrice() function utilizes the current price of the UniswapV3 pool which is susceptible to price manipulations and Flash-Loan price manipulation , permitting its users to artificially manipulation the asset prices.

Manually

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Change the code to be revamped to utilize the current tick rather than the actual sqrtPriceX96, ensuring that the code is not susceptible to in-tick price manipulation attacks and add TWAP mechanism or similar protection measure as it is presently insecure and can compromise user assets.

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-03-asymmetry/blob/main/contracts/SafEth/SafEth.sol#L71-L99
